lectures.title: Why insured people can look sicker: selection bias, decomposed
The Oregon lottery: what randomization actually buys you
The RAND Health Insurance Experiment: randomizing the price of care
Which average effect are you even estimating?
Nobody complies: intention-to-treat versus the effect of treatment
Instrumental variables and the LATE theorem
Selection on observables: matching, regression, and the leap of faith
Arrows or potential outcomes? Bad controls and colliders
Difference-in-differences and the parallel trends assumption
When treatment arrives at different times: staggered DiD in trouble
Regression discontinuity: what happens at your 65th birthday
Building a counterfactual state: synthetic control and Proposition 99
Reading a null: power, precision, and the Oregon blood-sugar result
Choosing a design, and turning an estimate into a policy

quiz.question: Maria's neighbour James has no coverage and 25 good days. What did insurance do for Maria?
choices: It cost her one good day
We can't tell from these numbers

quiz.question: The two sicker people signed up. Will the survey's gap, insured minus uninsured, come out above the true four days, below it, or about the same?
A hospital wants to know whether a follow-up phone call after discharge keeps patients from coming back. Which comparison answers it?
choices: Picked at random to be called, against not picked
Answered the call, against didn't answer
This year's patients, all called, against last year's

quiz.question: Suppose coverage did nothing at all, for anyone. What would the quick comparison show in this town?
Older people who get a flu shot die less often over the winter than those who don't. Which way does selection push that comparison?
A researcher adds controls, and the insured-minus-uninsured gap moves from minus four to zero. What has she learned?
choices: Only that the recorded differences mattered
That all the bias is now gone

quiz.question: Dee, Eli and Fay signed up. Covered average minus uncovered average: what will it come to?
A clinic can send a nurse to half its diabetic patients. Which way of choosing them makes the two columns independent of the choice?
choices: The nurses pick those who need it most
Patients who ask for a visit get one
A computer draws half the names

quiz.question: Suppose clerks quietly let people who phoned in on the first day jump the queue. Which row flags it?
choices: Neither: only the outcomes would show it

quiz.question: A trial's balance table has thirty rows. Two are starred, one tilted each way, and the joint test gives p = 0.4. What do you conclude?
choices: Drop the two starred rows and rerun

quiz.question: A city gives free bus passes by lottery to 2,000 of 6,000 applicants. The draw balances, and a year on, winners report more job interviews. What can you claim?
choices: Bus passes raise interviews for everyone in the city
The offer of a pass raised interviews among applicants like these
Nothing, since winners chose whether to use their passes

quiz.question: Compare what we can see: the Lenas' spending minus the Toms'. How will that gap compare with the true three hundred and fifty?
choices: Far above three hundred and fifty

quiz.question: Compared with families paying ninety-five percent of every bill, how much more did free-care families spend?
When a price made people use less care, which care did they give up?
A state adds a copay for doctor visits for low-income adults, many with high blood pressure. Which reading of RAND fits?
choices: Health won't change: RAND found no effect
Visits will fall, and blood pressure control may slip

quiz.question: After the voluntary sign-up, the state auto-enrols everyone still uninsured. How many good days does that buy per newly covered person?
A neighbouring state will cover all its uninsured, and four in five of them are the reluctant kind. About how many good days per person should it expect?

A job-training scheme was tested by lottery among unemployed people who applied for it, because they expected it to help. Now it becomes compulsory for everyone unemployed. Per person, what should the government expect?
choices: The same effect: the trial was randomized
A larger effect: more people take part

quiz.question: The enrolled were poorer and sicker than the winners who stayed out, and less likely to have a regular clinic on their own. So the twenty-point gap is…
choices: Smaller than what coverage did for them
Bigger than what coverage did for them
Exactly what coverage did, since the draw was random

quiz.question: A clinic offers free nicotine patches to a random half of its smokers; nobody else gets them. Only half of those offered use them. A year on, 20% of those offered have quit, against 14% of the rest. What did the patches do for those who used them?
Ana was not drawn, yet she is on Medicaid. Which kind of applicant is she?
Suppose the letter itself got never-takers a free check-up, saving each of them $13. What would the Wald ratio now report?
A clinic mails flu-shot reminders at random. Vaccinated: 50% with a reminder, 30% without. Caught flu: 9% against 10%. What does the Wald ratio say?
choices: Flu down 5 points, for everyone reminded
Flu down 5 points, for those the reminder moved

quiz.question: A study uses each doctor's choice for the previous patient, drug A or B, as an instrument for the drug the next patient gets. Which story would break the exclusion restriction?
choices: Doctors' habits decide which drug a patient gets
Which patient came before has nothing to do with this patient's health
Doctors who favour drug A also follow patients up more closely

quiz.question: A study instruments same-day heart surgery with weekend admission. The first-stage F is 12, and the estimate says surgery halves deaths. What should worry you most?
choices: The F should be above a hundred

quiz.question: Inside the row with no conditions on file, will the insured still look worse off than the uninsured?
With the third row dropped, whose effect does the plus two now describe?
choices: The two hundred in the first two rows

quiz.question: A clinic offers free diet coaching. Researchers compare patients who joined with non-joiners who match them on age, weight and diagnoses. What would most bias the result?
choices: Too few patients in the study
Joiners were already set on changing their habits
Both groups have the same average age

quiz.question: Among the admitted patients, which group is sicker?
Oregon's researchers wanted the effect of winning the lottery. Which of these could they safely control for?
choices: Household size on the sign-up form

quiz.question: Which assumption about Oregon's lottery can the graph's arrows not show?
choices: Winning affects health only through coverage
The lottery is unrelated to sickness
Winning never makes anyone less likely to enrol

quiz.question: Suppose the states that did not expand had fallen only from 37 to 33, while the expansion states still went from 33 to 21. What is the estimate?
From 2010 to 2013 the two groups moved in parallel. What does that show?
choices: No sign of diverging trends before 2014

quiz.question: A study compares hospital deaths in states that raised nurse staffing in 2016 with states that did not. Which finding would worry you most?
choices: The staffing states also opened trauma centres in 2016
The staffing states had higher death rates all along
Death rates fell in both groups

quiz.question: Every effect in the table is positive. What will two-way fixed effects report for $\hat\beta$?
Suppose Early's effect had stayed at 2 in its second year, with everything else the same. What would $\hat\beta$ be?
In the two-state table, which effects have a clean control, a state still untreated that year?
Every state adopts a nurse-staffing rule at some point between 2010 and 2020, and its effect on deaths builds over five years. Should you trust one two-way fixed effects number?
choices: Yes: the fixed effects absorb the timing
Yes, if the pre-period estimates look flat
No: late states are compared with early ones whose effects are still growing

quiz.question: Which comparison would isolate what Medicare does?
choices: A month short of 65 against a month past it

quiz.question: Suppose a state also gave everyone a free yearly check-up from their 65th birthday on. What would the step at 65 measure?
Suppose Medicare also brought milder cases into hospital after 65. Which way would that push the measured step in deaths?
If coverage had saved every one of those newly insured patients, how much of the drop of 1.1 points could that explain?
Why does widening the bandwidth change the estimate?
choices: It pulls in points far from 65, where a straight fit must approximate a curved relationship

quiz.question: Which running variable is vulnerable to manipulation?
choices: Reported income relative to a Medicaid eligibility threshold

quiz.question: In a fuzzy RD, the jump in Y is divided by what?
choices: The jump in the probability of treatment at the cutoff

quiz.question: As you widen the bandwidth, what happens?
Your plot is flat from h = 1 to 5, then slides steeply downward from 6 onward. What do you conclude?
choices: Local estimate is stable; the drift is curvature at wide windows
Report h = 9 — it is the most precise

quiz.question: A density with a spike just below the cutoff and a dip just above suggests what?
Which running variable is most vulnerable to manipulation?
choices: Self-reported income at an eligibility line
A lottery number drawn by the state

quiz.question: In this fuzzy design, what is being instrumented by what?
choices: Crossing the cutoff instruments for coverage

quiz.question: Whose effect is that 0.20?
choices: Those whose coverage the birthday itself changed

quiz.question: Suppose we used the 38-state average anyway, in a difference-in-differences. The effect it gives the tax would be…
Suppose a synthetic Texas, built to study a 1995 law, misses Texas's own sales before 1995 by twelve packs a year. What should we make of its gap after 1995?
choices: Little: the stand-in failed its main test
Half of it is the law's effect

quiz.question: A city's soda tax is studied with synthetic control and nine donor cities. Its gap is the most extreme of all ten. What is the smallest p-value placebo runs can give it?
In a cost per QALY figure, which input is a value judgement wearing a parameter's clothes?
choices: The effect of coverage on depression
The weight on a year lived with depression
The cost of enrolling one adult

quiz.question: Losing the lottery makes people seek free clinic care they'd otherwise skip. Which assumption breaks?
Which of these can you actually test in the data?
The ITT is about $195 a year and a quarter of those drawn enrolled. What is the LATE?
Whose effect is the Oregon LATE?
choices: Those whose enrollment the lottery changed

quiz.question: Which change moves the cost per QALY with no new data at all?
The $778 spending effect and the EQ-5D utility weight differ in kind. How?
choices: One is estimated, one is elicited preference
